The novel flying machine that is being built on Staten Island to try for the flight across the Atlantic. The machine is known as the Macleod Multiplane. It is an albatross in boat and wings. Has 18 wings, 9 on each side of a cylindrical shaped body. The wings are both concave and convex, each a parachute in itself. The wings graduate in size from 32 feet from tip to tip on the upper story to 28 feet on the second story and 24 feet on the third story, six wings to each story. All are six feet wide. The reason of all the secrecy that is maintained until the first few weeks of September was explained to The Daily Mirror yesterday.

No one is admitted into the secret chamber, and although some of the practical work is sometimes allotted to trusted employees, The Daily Mirror was told yesterday "they cannot guess in what way their individual work will be fitted into the outline of a gown."

"Models of new fashions must be shown to our exclusive customers before anyone else sees them," The Daily Mirror was told, "for if our new ideas were copied and became general our customers would not be likely to order them. They must have the new modes first. Afterwards if they are copied it does not matter."
Copyists are everywhere looking for ideas, listening for hints, and against these the great modistes have to protect themselves.
"COPIED MODES NOT WANTED."

"New fashions are usually a development or a slight alteration of the preceding fashions," said a representative of another firm. "This is the reason that a certain uniformity of modes emanates from the different dressmakers. This happens unless one modiste creates something startling that becomes a craze. There is a general feeling this year that there will be no decided change, although one can never say definitely.
"If it is found that a certain material is to be very fashionable, firms try to make a corner in it and buy up as much as possible, so that other firms have a difficulty in obtaining it,"

A feature of the lighter side of the Doncaster meeting was the appearance in the aerodrome yesterday of Mr. Edward Mines, with his curious - looking biplane. To the great amusement of everyone present the machine declined to rise, despite the fact that an effort was made to induce it to leave the ground by harnessing it to a motor-

car and dragging it rapidly along. (1) Mr. Mines in his aeroplane. It is not officially described in the programme, but has been alluded to at various times as "a coffee stall," "a band box," and "a meat safe." (2) The machine being dragged along by the motor-car.-(Daily Mirror photographs.)
